name: Tripeptide-10 citrulline
evidenceNote: The case for it rests on the maker's lab tests of collagen fibers and one small randomized skin study of 24 volunteers, six per group, measuring wrinkle depth with an imaging device. There are no larger or independent controlled trials.
summary: Tripeptide-10 citrulline is a skincare peptide built to mimic decorin, a protein that keeps collagen fibers orderly. Evidence is lab work and one small study.
keyTakeaway: Tripeptide-10 citrulline is a short synthetic peptide used in anti-aging creams and serums, sold to formulators as Decorinyl. Despite the name, it is four amino acids long. It was designed to copy the part of decorin, a skin protein, that binds collagen and keeps its fibers even. In the developer's lab tests it made collagen fibers thinner and more uniform. One randomized study of 24 volunteers reported smoother skin surface measurements after 20 to 60 days. As a cosmetic ingredient it needs no FDA approval, and whether enough of it passes the skin barrier to reach collagen in the dermis has not been shown.

blocks.text: Tripeptide-10 citrulline is a synthetic peptide made for skincare. Its name is an INCI name, the standardized label used on cosmetic ingredient lists, and it is a little misleading: the molecule is actually a tetrapeptide, a chain of four amino acids, one of which is citrulline [1]. It was first described in a 2008 paper by its developers [1] and is supplied to brands under the trade name Decorinyl [3].

Reviews of cosmetic peptides group it with the signal peptides, ingredients meant to send messages to skin cells or tissue rather than simply moisturize [3]. A 2026 safety paper places it among the matrikines, peptides that mimic fragments of the skin's own structural proteins [5].

Collagen gives the dermis (the thick layer under the skin's surface) its strength, but how well collagen works depends partly on how its fibers are arranged. Decorin, a protein that coats collagen fibrils, helps control their assembly and prevents them from clumping into irregular bundles. As skin ages, functional decorin declines, and collagen fibers become disorganized, which reduces the skin's tensile strength [1].

The developers identified two short sequences in decorin that bind collagen, engineered variants with stronger binding, and screened a library of candidates in a test of collagen fiber formation. Tripeptide-10 citrulline performed best. In those lab experiments it behaved like decorin, regulating fiber formation and making the fibers thinner and more uniform in diameter [1]. The aim, in the authors' framing, was collagen quality rather than quantity [1].

No, and as a cosmetic ingredient it does not need to be. Under US law, cosmetic products other than color additives can be sold without FDA approval [4]. A product's claims matter, though: if a label says it changes the structure or function of the body, the FDA can treat it as a drug, even if it is marketed as a cosmetic [4].

Independent safety review is also limited. A 2026 overview of cosmetic peptide safety listed the peptides assessed by the Cosmetic Ingredient Review expert panel, the main US body that evaluates cosmetic ingredients, and tripeptide-10 citrulline was not among them [5].

sections.heading: What is tripeptide-10 citrulline used for?

blocks.text: It appears in anti-aging skincare marketed for firmness, suppleness and fine lines. The original paper pitched it as a way to improve skin suppleness through better cohesion of collagen fibers [1]. It is often formulated alongside other peptides, such as acetyl hexapeptide-3, and one of the few human studies tested exactly that pairing [2].

The foundation is the 2008 paper from its developers, which reported only lab results on collagen fiber formation, without any testing on human skin [1]. Lab effects on isolated collagen do not show that a cream reaches the dermis, where collagen lives.

The only controlled human study found was published in 2017. Twenty-four healthy volunteers were randomized to four groups of six: tripeptide-10 citrulline alone, acetyl hexapeptide-3 alone, the two combined, or neither, for 60 days. Skin surface roughness was measured with an imaging device, and water loss through the skin with a second instrument. The groups using tripeptide-10 citrulline showed some significant differences in roughness measures at 20 and 60 days, and the authors described this as clinical evidence of anti-wrinkle activity, while noting that the combination's mechanism was unclear [2].

blocks.text: Six people per group is too few to draw firm conclusions, and the study measured skin surface texture rather than wrinkles as graded by experts or by users. A broader problem applies to all cosmetic peptides: their size and water-loving chemistry make it hard to cross the skin's outer barrier. Reviews put the ideal size for skin penetration under about 500 daltons, while this peptide weighs roughly 531 [3].

No specific adverse effects have been reported in the published studies of tripeptide-10 citrulline, but those studies were small and short [1][2]. As with any skincare ingredient, irritation or allergic reactions are possible, often from other components of the formula. Because it has not been through a Cosmetic Ingredient Review assessment, there is no independent panel finding on safe concentrations [5].

Most of the cosmetic peptides that panel has reviewed were judged safe as currently used. The 2026 framework argues for adding computer-based screening to the standard checks on irritation, skin sensitization and whole-body toxicity when new peptides are assessed [5].
